title: Pension: East rural farmers and fishers
body: The single largest lookalike segment in this whole analysis - roughly 635,000 rural, low-income farming/fishing adults, mostly Ubudehe 2, who score as closely resembling existing RSSB/Ejo Heza holders. The surprise: they're not held back by awareness - about 76% already say they understand how insurance works, versus only ~45% of actual pension holders in this same archetype, and they use mobile money *more* often than holders do. The barrier looks less like "doesn't know what a pension is" and more like distribution reach or a trigger to actually sign up.
channel: Village-level Ejo Heza savings agents and VUP touchpoints - this group already engages with mobile money, so mobile-linked sign-up (not a new physical branch) is the natural channel.
product_angle: Ejo Heza matched-savings, pitched as a low, flexible contribution rather than a formal pension product - fits a farming/fishing income pattern better than a fixed monthly premium.

title: Pension: Kigali urban salaried professionals
body: Roughly 170,000 affluent, urban, salaried Kigali adults who look almost identical to people who already hold RSSB or private pensions - understanding, awareness and mobile money use are all within a few points of the holder population. This is the closest thing to a pure "quick win" in the data: they're not missing information, they likely just haven't been offered the product through the right channel yet.
channel: Employer payroll partnerships and bank-linked sign-up - this group is already banked and salaried, so the friction is almost certainly distribution, not persuasion.
product_angle: RSSB voluntary top-up or a private pension product marketed alongside existing salaried benefits, not a savings-literacy campaign.

title: Insurance: East rural farmers and fishers
body: About 145,000 rural, low-income farming/fishing adults who resemble insurance holders. Same pattern as the pension segment above: roughly 95% say they understand insurance, versus ~63% of actual holders in this archetype, and awareness of microinsurance and life insurance is also higher among the lookalikes. Roughly a quarter are more than 60 minutes from the nearest insurance branch - physical distribution gap, not an information gap.
channel: Bundle with agricultural input/cooperative schemes they already use, rather than a standalone insurance sales push.
product_angle: Crop/livestock micro-insurance - the one product type directly relevant to this livelihood, and currently under-distributed relative to how many people already understand the concept.

title: Insurance: Kigali urban salaried professionals
body: About 94,000 affluent, urban Kigali professionals who look like insurance holders on paper. Again, awareness is not the gap - roughly 92% understand insurance and 91% are aware of life insurance specifically, both higher than the holder population. For this group the likely blocker is a concrete offer or price point, not education.
channel: Direct digital/bank-linked distribution - this segment already uses mobile money and lives near an insurance branch, so access isn't the constraint either.
product_angle: Life or credit-life insurance bundled with an existing bank/SACCO loan product, targeting the moment of a financial decision rather than a cold sell.

title: Pension: North rural farmers and fishers
body: About 107,000 rural adults in Ubudehe 3 (slightly better off than the East rural segment above) who resemble pension holders. Awareness and understanding here are closer between holders and lookalikes than in the other segments, suggesting this group is genuinely on the fence rather than mismatched - a smaller but very reachable pool.
channel: Same village-agent / VUP channel as the East rural segment, but this group's slightly higher Ubudehe category means a modestly higher contribution tier may be viable.
product_angle: Ejo Heza standard tier, positioned alongside the existing VUP relationship this group already has.
